overview: The Jin dynasty briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but internal weakness and uprisings by the peoples of the north led to the loss of the north in 316. The Eastern Jin survived in the south as a center of Chinese culture.

items.text: Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion, the most admired piece of Chinese calligraphy, at a spring gathering of poets.
Landscape painting begins to emerge as an independent art form; Gu Kaizhi paints the Admonitions scroll.
Huiyuan founds a Buddhist community on Mount Lu; translation projects and monasteries multiply.
The monk Faxian sets out for India to collect Buddhist texts, and returns by sea fifteen years later.
The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, of the Wei to Jin transition, exemplify literati withdrawal and philosophical debate.
Eastern Jin preserved Chinese high culture in the south while the north underwent ethnic mixing.

fall.text: The last Eastern Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, a powerful general who founded the Liu Song dynasty.
